claims.text: The baseline alloy has composition Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 in atomic percent.
The current Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 formulation has limited amorphous retention.
The baseline alloy has a complicated and unstable thermal response during reheating.
The proposed intervention is to add approximately 2–4 atomic percent boron to the alloy.
Adding 2–4 atomic percent boron will improve the alloy's glass-forming ability.
Adding 2–4 atomic percent boron will enhance the thermal stability of the amorphous state during reheating.
Boron addition will enhance atomic-size mismatch in the amorphous structure.
Boron addition will increase topological disorder in the amorphous structure.
Boron is a metalloid with a significantly smaller atomic size than the transition-metal constituents of the alloy.
The smaller boron atoms will increase atomic-level packing frustration.
Increased packing frustration will depress crystal-nucleation rates.
Increased packing frustration will reduce atomic mobility.
Reduced nucleation and atomic mobility will stabilize the amorphous phase during cooling and delay crystallization during reheating.
The boron-modified alloy will retain a higher amorphous fraction after solidification than the boron-free baseline.
The boron-modified alloy will have a higher crystallization-onset temperature than the boron-free baseline.
The beneficial effect will diminish if the boron content exceeds an optimal range.
At sufficiently extreme cooling rates, kinetic effects may override the proposed boron-stabilization mechanism.
At reheating conditions far beyond the typical analysis range, boron addition may not prevent crystallization.
